t: Longest Arithmetic Sequence After Changing At Most One Element
o: Replace at most one element with any integer, then take the longest arithmetic (constant-difference) contiguous subarray. In [9,7,5,10,1] replacing the 10 with 3 joins the left run [9,7,5] (diff -2) with [1], giving length 5. In [1,2,6,7] the best is length 3. Precompute for every index the longest arithmetic run ending and starting there, then try bridging across each replaced position.
k: left[i] = longest arithmetic suffix ending at i; right[i] = longest arithmetic prefix starting at i — both computable in one pass each.
Replacing nums[i] can (a) extend the left run by 1, (b) extend the right run by 1, or (c) bridge both sides if the differences agree (with special handling when a side has length 1).
Bridging with a length-1 neighbor requires the far element to fit: nums[i+1]-nums[i-1] must equal twice the known difference.

a.i: Build left[] and right[] via simple recurrences. For each candidate replaced index i, combine: extension gives left[i-1]+1 or right[i+1]+1; a full bridge needs the left diff and right diff to match, or, when one side is a single element, the midpoint condition nums[i+1]-nums[i-1] == 2*d. Take the max over all candidates and all untouched runs.
s: Compute left[i] (extend if nums[i]-nums[i-1] equals the previous difference) and right[i] analogously.
For each i: consider left[i-1]+1, right[i+1]+1, and bridge cases (equal diffs, or single-sided midpoint checks, or length-3 when both sides are single elements).
a.t: O(n) — two linear DP passes plus one linear enumeration

w: Enumerating the replaced index and bridging precomputed runs is the clean interview solution; trying all replacements naively is O(n^2). Pitfalls: the single-element-neighbor midpoint condition (nums[i+1]-nums[i-1] == 2*d), replacements at the array ends, and remembering the no-replacement answer max(left). Follow-up: allow up to k changes (DP over positions with run states), or longest geometric subarray.
